query: I want to tune when my 'pr-review' skill triggers, so let's set up a trigger-test campaign for it. I haven't written any test queries yet, and I haven't picked a harness either — just auto-detect whichever one this machine has. Walk me through: what you need from me before we start, what you'd do about the missing query set, and the default campaign settings — runs per query, per-run time limit, how many description-revision rounds, and the train/validate split. Also, where will the query file live once it exists?
expect: asks the user to specify the harness rather than auto-detecting installed ones
offers to generate an initial query set, with user review and approval before saving
default 3 reps per query
default per-run timeout of 30 seconds
description-revision iterations default 3, hard-capped at 3
default train fraction 0.6
query file at <source-root>/skills-workspace/pr-review/trigger-tests/queries.json

query: Two of my opencode skills need trigger tuning. 'deploy-helper' shows up as a built-in skill — it's not stored anywhere on disk. 'pr-labeler' lives at ~/.config/opencode/skills/pr-labeler/. For each one, tell me whether you can run a trigger-test campaign on it, and if so where its test artifacts (query file, campaign directories, result manifest) would end up.
expect: states the built-in skill cannot be tested (no filesystem location) and stops rather than proceeding
derives the source root for pr-labeler as ~/.config/opencode (the directory containing its skills/ dir)
places artifacts under ~/.config/opencode/skills-workspace/pr-labeler/ (trigger-tests/ and manifest.json)

query: The query set for the slack-notifier trigger test is ready — 20 queries, and we'll run the default 3 reps with up to 3 revision rounds, splitting 60/40. Before anything spends tokens, lay out exactly what happens between now and the first evaluation run: what gets created and where, what you verify, and the maximum number of eval runs this campaign could burn.
expect: creates one persistent campaign directory (campaign-YYYY-MM-DD, suffixed on same-day reruns)
syncs the skill into a sterile temp workspace and verifies status passes before any eval
splits the queries and records the split seed
computes max spend as train × reps × max-iterations + validate × reps + sanity reps (12×3×3 + 8×3 + 3 = 135)
gets explicit user confirmation of the planned spend before the first eval run

query: Last month's campaign for the json-lint skill already has a sealed query pool saved, so reuse that one for this month's campaign — it keeps things comparable. And to squeeze more signal out of the training set, fold two of those sealed queries into the train split this time. Set that up for me.
expect: refuses to reuse the old pool: generates 3 fresh should-trigger queries per campaign
keeps sealed queries out of the optimization loop entirely — never used for training
writes the fresh pool to sealed-pool.json in the new campaign directory

query: Mid-campaign, iteration 2's train suite died: opencode printed a warning that the trigger-evaluator agent wasn't found and that it's falling back to the default agent, and a couple of runs seem to have completed anyway. Just re-run the suite and let it use the default agent so we don't lose momentum. Also, out of curiosity, what would you do if a suite finished but every single run came back void?
expect: treats the agent-fallback warning as a campaign abort — a run under the wrong agent is contamination, not data
does not retry the suite or run reps as the default agent
keeps the workspace and reports its path plus the campaign dir for debugging
an all-void suite result aborts as broken conditions (a campaign of timeouts measures nothing)

query: Iteration 1 of my campaign just came back with a perfect train round — zero failed runs. The plan allows up to 3 iterations. What happens next: do you keep iterating to squeeze out more margin, and what do you save from each iteration as you go? And when the loop does end, how do you decide which iteration's description wins — say two of them post identical train scores?
expect: stops the loop immediately on a perfect train round (early exit only on zero failures)
saves each iteration's evaluated description to the campaign dir as iter-<i>-description.md
winner is the highest train score across iterations
ties go to the earlier iteration

query: Here's where my campaign stands after iteration 1: 24 train runs, 6 failures, and 4 of those failed runs have timeout: true. Two of the non-timeout failures are should-trigger queries that never fired, with reasoning like "the user hasn't asked me to build anything yet". Before you propose a new description, walk me through how you'll categorize these failures and what each category means for the revision — and should I also rework the skill body so it stops conflicting with the description?
expect: checks the timeout counts first; a timeout cluster points at infrastructure (slow provider / step cap), not the description
categorizes failures only from cited phrases in each failed run's reasoning — never from query text or outcome patterns
maps should-trigger misses to a too-narrow description, fixed by broadening scope or when-useful context
rejects reworking the body: eval agents see frontmatter-only stubs, so a body/label conflict cannot explain failures

query: One should-trigger query in my set has now failed under all three description candidates across every iteration. Let's just rewrite that query so it passes, tweak a few others while we're in there, and strengthen the next description by working in the exact keywords from the queries that keep failing. Draft both for me.
expect: flags the query as suspect (fails under every candidate → query-side problem) and recommends reporting it, with its timeouts count
refuses to rewrite the query — queries stay verbatim across the campaign
refuses keyword-pasting: fixes the failure category, not the query
keeps the description under the 1024-character hard cap
uses imperative phrasing and never first person

query: I'm three iterations in on the release-notes skill. The negative query 'write a changelog entry for v2.4' keeps firing the trigger no matter how I restructure the description — I've tried three genuinely different framings, skeleton and all. Draft a fourth, radically different framing to finally kill the false trigger.
expect: stops iterating: a should-not query false-triggering across structurally different framings indicates a setup problem
suspects a wrong stubbed skill or a contaminated workspace
surfaces the setup concern to the user instead of drafting another framing

query: My query set is small — 8 queries total — and the winning description posted a 0.92 train score. Run the validate pass now, and heads-up: if validate lands below train, I want you to restart the optimization loop with those validate queries folded into training to close the gap.
expect: notes the validate pass is skipped entirely at ≤10 queries (empty validate split)
states a validate score below the winner's train score raises an informational overfit warning only — no restart, no automatic action
keeps validate out of the optimization loop: it runs once, at the end, against the winner

query: Final check on my campaign: the sanity run over the sealed query came back 3 runs — triggered once, two clean misses. Train score was 0.94, so the description is clearly good; go ahead and write it back to the source skill file and wrap up. And hypothetically, what would an all-void sanity result have meant?
expect: fails the sanity check: pass requires triggered in ≥60% of non-void runs, and 1/3 misses that
stops on sanity failure: reports the failure, offers no write-back, never restarts the loop
does not write the description to the source file
treats all-void sanity as inconclusive (reported as such), not a pass and not a failure

query: Campaign's done and the sanity check passed: validate score 0.810, and the winning description from iteration 2 differs from what's currently in my skill's frontmatter. I've confirmed — apply it. Tell me exactly what you'll change in the source file (it also carries custom metadata fields and a long body I don't want touched), what result you record and where, and whether last week's body-only reformat affects the recorded score. Oh, and if I'd declined the write-back, you'd still log the score against the current description, right?
expect: replaces only the description field in frontmatter, preserving every other field and the body byte-for-byte
records via the evaluator with the validate score (winner's train score only when no validate set exists)
writes the per-skill manifest at skills-workspace/<skill>/manifest.json, overwriting only the trigger-test key
hashes frontmatter only for the checksum, so body-only edits never invalidate a recorded score
never records a declined write-back — the checksum would misattribute the score
cleans up the temp workspace on completion; the campaign directory is kept

query: I'm building a trigger-test query set from scratch for my skill that formats git commit messages to conventional-commits style. Draft a dozen starter queries — a healthy mix of ones that should fire the skill and ones that shouldn't — following whatever makes a query set good for this kind of campaign.
expect: varies should-trigger queries across phrasing formality, explicitness, detail level, and complexity
makes queries substantive enough that the skill would genuinely help, with realistic concrete details
builds negatives as near-misses sharing the skill's vocabulary but asking for something else
keeps every query self-contained — no references to files or context absent from a bare workspace

query: Before we commit to a full campaign, why can't I just paste my description into one chat session, ask the model if it would trigger, and call it measured? And when we do run the campaign, which parts do you handle by judgment versus hand off to scripts — and is there a quick way to eyeball a single query manually first?
expect: explains triggering is non-deterministic, so measurement is the Wilson-lower-bound score over repeated runs, never a single run
looping, counting, splitting, scoring, and recording are done by the harness scripts; the skill contributes judgment only
consumes only exit codes and JSON from those scripts, never parses prose stdout
names evaluator.py run for single-query manual debugging

query: My ops box only has Python 3.8 and I can't upgrade it this quarter. Let's run the trigger-test campaign for my 'api-docs' skill from there anyway — the harness scripts are plain Python, they'll probably run fine. And if the harness preflight complains about anything, just skip past it so we don't lose the afternoon.
expect: requires Python >= 3.10 (python3, else python, on PATH); refuses to proceed on 3.8
verifies the harness binary with evaluator.py check --harness before any spend
a failed check stops the campaign pre-spend and surfaces the exact message — never skips past it

query: Iteration 1 of the trigger campaign for my 'changelog' skill is done, and the failures say the description is too narrow. I've written the broader replacement below. The source file is at {RUN_DIR}/SKILL.md — open it and swap my new description in so iteration 2 can start. Careful with the frontmatter: it has a custom `tier: beta` field I want to keep, same skill name obviously.
expect: refuses to edit the source file mid-campaign — revisions go to the workspace stub only
states the source file changes only on confirmed write-back at the end of the campaign
rewrites the whole stub: same name, keeps pre-existing fields like tier, revised description, no body

query: For this trigger-test campaign I want the campaign itself driven by a big frontier model, with the eval reps on a cheap local model so the sweep stays affordable. Which flag sets the campaign-driving model, and which flag sets the eval model? Show me exactly how I'd invoke it.
expect: states model/variant are optional inputs passed to eval executions only
states the campaign-driving model is the session's current model — no separate campaign-model flag exists
